extracted.intended_audience: scientific colleagues (botanists, geologists) and editors; historians of science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards, embedded in Darwin's letters, for compiling and using floras, for testing biogeographical hypotheses (dispersal vs former continental connection), and for decisions about publishing preliminary scientific sketches versus full works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Append geographic origin labels in floras
rubrics_metrics.description: Append (Eu) in brackets to any European plant in a flora.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin: adding a short bracketed label (e.g. 'Eu') to indicate a plant's origin gives readers a quick notion of range and lets beginners and inquirers see which plants are indigenous or European without taking much space. (He notes Dr. Gray adopted this in subsequent editions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Give habitats and regional occurrence where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply habitats and occurrence data for plants found west of the Rocky Mountains and for those found in Eastern Asia (e.g., Yenesei partition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin suggests including habitats for regions outside the author's immediate area when possible, because east–west and Eurasia–Greenland–Western Europe comparisons help infer directionality of migration; he acknowledges it may be too troublesome in some manuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report whole-number counts as well as proportional fractions for families
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish both the absolute (whole) numbers of species in each family and their proportions (fractions) relative to the whole flora.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues that without whole numbers one cannot judge how close proportions truly are between two countries; he gives examples (Umbelliferae 36/1798 = 1/49) and recommends whole numbers in addition to lowest fractions to assess similarity robustly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculate proportion of species to genera
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the average number of species per genus for the flora (species:genus ratio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin presumes authors will report this statistic as it helps characterize the flora's structure; he notes he has already done this for himself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify species into comparative groups for floristic analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide species into three groups: (a) species common to the Old World, stating numbers common to Europe and Asia; (b) indigenous species but belonging to genera found in the Old World; (c) species belonging to genera confined to America / the New World.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin recommends this tripartite division to give a clear idea of the flora's affinities and to aid speculation about means of transport and historical connections; he also suggests noting genera common in the Old World but absent in the study area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark 'close species' in floras (flag ambiguous taxa)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify species that one botanist regards as specifically distinct but which another good botanist might regard as a race or variety, or species that are difficult to discriminate even when well known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin defines 'close species' and asks that such taxa be marked (e.g., with a cross on proof-sheets) so they can be compared across different floras to see whether the same genera tend to have 'close species'; he admits the category is vague but useful for comparative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explicit statement of scope and limitations for preliminary essays
rubrics_metrics.description: If publishing a preliminary sketch rather than the full work, make it a thin, modest volume focused on main agency (selection) and a few leading features and difficulties, and state in a Preface that the work is not strictly scientific and that full references will follow in a larger work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin wrestles with the trade-off: sketches can elicit useful criticism but risk spreading incomplete conclusions or reducing novelty of a later larger work. He advises modesty, clear declaration of limits, and including only one or two memory-based examples if references cannot be provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support propositions with an array of facts; avoid unreferenced assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every scientific proposition requires a substantial array of facts and references; a resume without exact references is 'dreadfully unphilosophical.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin emphasizes that honest scientific practice requires giving the evidence for claims; while a sketch may be tolerable for soliciting feedback, serious claims should ultimately be supported by detailed facts and citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test evolutionary/biogeographical hypotheses across multiple independent lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate hypotheses (e.g., species descent, migration) by checking whether they explain and are consistent with general propositions in geographical distribution, geological history, affinities, fossil record, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin's methodology: assume the hypothesis provisionally if it explains many otherwise inexplicable facts, then test against as many well-established propositions as possible; use concordance across lines (distribution, geology, affinities) as support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require weighty, multifaceted evidence before inferring former continental connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer broad continental extensions (land-bridges/continents spanning oceans during recent times) on the basis of single or equivocal lines of evidence; demand strong corroboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin lists reasons for skepticism about recent continental extensions: (a) lack of secondary/palaeozoic rock on islands far from mainlands, (b) the generally volcanic nature of oceanic islands vs non-volcanic continental mountain ranges, (c) differences in faunal/floral composition (absence of mammals, batrachians), and (d) sea depth as a barrier. He argues these factors together reduce the plausibility of recent continuous land connections and recommends high evidentiary standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use island geology (volcanic vs continental rock) as a test of former land continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the geological character of islands (mostly volcanic) with that of continental mountain peaks (largely non-volcanic) when assessing whether an island is a last wreck of a continent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin reasons that if oceanic islands were remnants of continents, we should find continental-type rocks (syenite, diorite, porphyry) rather than recent volcanic material; the predominance of volcanic islands argues against many supposed recent continental connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fossil and faunal distribution differences to infer long-standing separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in recent and miocene (or eocene) shell faunas on opposite sides of continents, and the distinctness of living shells and extinct marsupials in Australia, indicate long-term separation of continental areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites distinct fossil/molluscan records and extinct faunas as evidence that continents have been in their broad positions since at least the miocene, and that such palaeontological data should weigh heavily against claims of recent massive geographic rearrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat coincidences in proportional family counts cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent near-identity in proportional numbers of families between two floras may be accidental; check other families and compute proportions across many families before inferring historical connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin gives examples where one family's proportions corresponded closely across regions but others did not, leading him to conclude some coincidences are probably accidental; hence broad, multivariate checks are necessary.
